## TL;DR

Fixed the Hub server list pull-to-refresh lifecycle and replaced the rotating text glyph with a centered SVG loader. Pulling now fills a pink-to-purple circular progress arc, while a refresh uses the same balanced circle with a rotating arc. Releasing the finger clears gesture progress immediately; the `refreshing` prop alone controls the loader after that point. The indicator remains in a stable list slot and fades/scales in and out so its appearance does not insert or remove list rows. Reduced-motion preferences disable the motion. A component test covers releasing while the asynchronous refresh remains active and then completing the refresh.

The required changed-path check passed on the final tree, including build, TypeScript validation, scoped tests, and the browser gate.

## Work and rationale

The original component tracked a drag distance in `pullDistance`, and the template showed the indicator whenever either that value was positive or the parent reported `refreshing`. `onTouchEnd` only cleared the drag distance if no refresh was active. This meant lifting a finger during a refresh left gesture state behind. Even once the parent cleared `refreshing`, that stale positive distance could keep the indicator mounted.

I changed the touch-end handler to always clear gesture progress. That keeps the state machine straightforward: touch movement owns progress before release, and the parent-owned `refreshing` prop owns loading after release. The touch-cancel event already shares the same handler, so cancellation now clears progress through the same path. A sub-threshold pull also reaches touch end and clears through this handler. When a refresh ends or rejects, the parent refresh function already resets its busy flag in `finally`, and the underlying server reachability function applies a ten-second abort timeout to each check. Those existing guarantees meant no additional refresh orchestration or timeout policy was needed.

The old glyph was replaced with an inline SVG containing a circular track and progress arc. SVG keeps the shape rotationally balanced and lets the progress arc rotate around the exact center. A gradient from pink to purple gives the loader the requested Hub styling. During a pull, the arc length reflects the tracked pull distance. During loading, the same arc rotates continuously. The list item stays mounted at a fixed height with stable margins; visibility uses opacity and a small transform transition rather than conditionally inserting or removing an element. This gives the indicator a soft entrance and exit without pushing the first server row when visibility changes. The existing `prefers-reduced-motion` media query now disables both the transition and the spinner animation.

The test simulates a downward gesture, updates the component to the active-refresh state before releasing the touch, and confirms the indicator remains visible while refreshing. It then marks refreshing complete and confirms that the visible state clears. The adjacent existing indicator test was updated to check visibility rather than DOM existence because the stable layout slot remains mounted even when hidden.

## Approaches tried

The first implementation replaced the spinner glyph and reset pull distance on every release, while keeping the indicator conditionally mounted. That would have fixed stale progress, but a conditional list child could change the list's content geometry and move rows when shown or hidden. The final version keeps an empty-height slot instead, animating its content while preserving row placement. This also makes the same slot available to display pull progress before the refresh begins.

The first test pass exposed two test-harness mismatches: an existing test assumed the hidden indicator would be removed from the DOM, and the Vue Test Utils helper's inferred prop type did not include the optional prop passed through a generic mount helper. I revised the existing expectation to check the visibility class, and used a narrow type assertion on `setProps` calls in the new test. The first test run also caught that extracting `setProps` into a local function loses its `this` binding. Keeping calls on `wrapper.setProps` resolved that issue.

## Challenges and blockers

No product decision or external dependency was needed. The main design constraint was satisfying two requirements together: visible progress while pulling and no list jump when the indicator appears or leaves. A permanently allocated indicator slot meets both, but it does mean the list always reserves the same small vertical region. Its size is fixed and shared between idle, pulling, and refreshing states, so the rows do not move as a gesture changes state.

The initial scoped check correctly caught the visibility and method-binding test assumptions described above. After correcting those issues, the required check passed. The build emitted existing bundler warnings about externalized Node modules, a deep selector, and large chunks; none were errors and the browser gate exited successfully. There were no device-level interactions in this session, so no claim is made about physical-device QA.

## Key learnings

For pull-to-refresh components, gesture progress and refresh progress have separate owners and should not be conflated. Clear gesture state at the release/cancel boundary, then let the parent loading state control the active loader. A stable layout slot can make animation smoother and prevent list movement while still allowing gesture progress to be shown. Tests for transitioned UI should assert whether the UI is visible, not whether an element exists, when stable mounting is an intentional part of the layout.
